title: Parables of the Kingdom and the Storm Stilled
summary: Teaching from a boat, Jesus tells the parable of the sower and explains privately that the mystery of the kingdom is given to his followers while outsiders hear only riddles. He adds sayings about a lamp and a measure and two more seed parables, the seed that grows by itself and the mustard seed. That evening, crossing the lake, a fierce storm threatens to swamp the boat, and Jesus, woken from sleep, rebukes the wind and the waves, leaving his terrified disciples asking who he is.
story:
Chapter 3 ended with a divided response to Jesus: crowds flocked to him, his family came to take custody of him because they thought he was out of his mind (3:21), and scribes from Jerusalem said he drove out demons by the prince of demons (3:22). It closed with a new definition of family: those seated around him, doing the will of God, are his mother and brothers, while his relatives stand outside (3:31-35). Chapter 4 explains that divided response. The parable of the sower describes a word that meets hard, shallow, crowded, and good soil, and the rest of Mark shows each of those responses in action: opponents who never let the word in, crowds who welcome Jesus and melt away, a rich man choked by his wealth (10:22), and a few who bear fruit. The chapter also marks a turn toward the disciples as the ones who receive private explanation, the insiders to whom the mystery is given.

Then the story moves from teaching to action. The storm scene is the first of three boat scenes (4:35-41, 6:45-52, 8:14-21) in which the disciples are alone with Jesus on the lake and fail to understand him, and it opens a run of four mighty works (the storm, the Gerasene demoniac, the bleeding woman, and Jairus's daughter) that answer the question it raises: “Who is this, that even the wind and the sea obey Him?” That question governs the first half of Mark until Peter answers it at Caesarea Philippi (8:29).
historical:
The Sea of Galilee is a freshwater lake about thirteen miles long and eight miles wide at its widest, lying roughly 700 feet (about 210 meters) below sea level in a basin ringed by hills. Josephus, who commanded Jewish forces in Galilee in AD 66 and 67, gives its breadth as forty stadia and its length as 140 and praises its sweet water and its fish (Jewish War 3.506-508). Cool air pouring down through the valleys and off the Golan heights can meet the warm air over the water and raise sudden, violent storms, a danger local fishermen knew well. Mark calls it a sea (thalassa), as the Hebrew Bible calls it the Sea of Chinnereth (Numbers 34:11); Luke, writing for readers who knew the Mediterranean, calls it a lake (limnē).

In January 1986, during a drought that lowered the lake, two brothers from Kibbutz Ginosar found the remains of a wooden boat in the mud of the northwest shore. Excavated in eleven days by Israel's Department of Antiquities under Shelley Wachsmann, it is about 8.3 meters (27 feet) long and 2.3 meters (7.5 feet) wide, built of cedar and oak planks joined with mortise and tenon, and dated by radiocarbon to about 40 BC plus or minus eighty years and by pottery and construction to between about 50 BC and AD 50. It is now displayed at Ginosar. It shows the kind of boat the disciples used: large enough for a crew and passengers, with a stern platform under which a steersman sat and where a man could sleep, and Wachsmann's suggestion that the cushion of verse 38 was a ballast sandbag stored there fits Mark's definite article, ‘the cushion’.

The parables reflect the agricultural economy of Galilee under Herod Antipas, who ruled the region from 4 BC to AD 39 and rebuilt Sepphoris and founded Tiberias as his capitals (Josephus, Antiquities 18.27, 18.36-38). Most villagers worked small plots, often stony hillside terraces crossed by footpaths, and many farmed land they did not own, paying rents and taxes in kind. A good or bad harvest could decide whether a household survived the year. Early tradition, recorded by Papias (in Eusebius, Church History 3.39.15) and later writers, connects Mark with Peter and places the Gospel in Rome in the 60s, after Nero's persecution (Tacitus, Annals 15.44); others argue for Syria or Galilee. On either view, Mark's first readers knew trouble and persecution because of the word (verse 17) and knew what it was to feel that Jesus was asleep in the storm.
cultural:
Seed was scattered by hand from a bag or the fold of a garment, and some inevitably fell on the beaten path, on patches where limestone lay just below a thin skin of soil, or among the roots of thorns. Joachim Jeremias argued in The Parables of Jesus that Palestinian farmers sowed first and plowed afterward, pointing to the order of labors in m. Shabbat 7:2, so that sowing on the path was not careless; K. D. White and others replied that the evidence points both ways. The Book of Jubilees (11:11), a second-century BC retelling of Genesis, tells how Mastema, the chief of the evil spirits, sent birds to eat the seed before it could be plowed in, an image close to Mark's reading of the birds as Satan (verse 15). As for the harvest, the Roman writer Varro (On Agriculture 1.44.2) says that in parts of Italy seed returned ten or fifteen for one and that a hundred for one was reported only for exceptional land, including the district of Gadara just southeast of the lake; Isaac's hundredfold in Genesis 26:12 is a sign that the Lord blessed him. So thirty, sixty, and a hundred are not fantasy, but together they describe a harvest far beyond what the losses in verses 4 to 7 would lead a farmer to expect.

A parable (parabolē, ‘something set alongside’) belongs to the wide Hebrew category of mashal, which covers proverbs (1 Kings 4:32), taunts (Isaiah 14:4), riddles, allegories (Ezekiel 17:2), and illustrative stories such as Nathan's parable of the ewe lamb (2 Samuel 12:1-7). The rabbis later told hundreds of meshalim, many beginning ‘to what may the matter be compared’, which is close to the form of verse 30; David Flusser's study of the rabbinic parables (1981) showed how much Jesus' parables share with that tradition, though the written rabbinic collections are later than the Gospels. A parable draws on ordinary life to say something about God and leaves the hearer to finish the thought.

The household lamp was a small clay vessel holding olive oil and a wick, set on a stand to light a one-room house. The ‘basket’ (modios, from the Latin modius) was a grain measure of a little under nine liters, which could be turned over to put out or hide a flame. The saying about the measure was proverbial: the Mishnah states the same principle, that by the measure with which a person measures it is measured to him, and illustrates it from Samson and Absalom (m. Sotah 1:7-8). The mustard was probably black mustard (Brassica nigra), which grows wild around the lake and can reach two or three meters in a season. Its seed was the rabbis' standard for the smallest perceptible amount, as when the Mishnah speaks of a drop of blood the size of a mustard seed (m. Niddah 5:2), and the Roman naturalist Pliny the Elder notes that once mustard is sown it is hard to get rid of (Natural History 19.170-171). Finally, a teacher asleep while his students bail water would have startled no one; the scandal lies in their words, since a disciple's rebuke of his teacher was a serious breach of honor.
literary:
Mark 4 is the first extended block of Jesus' teaching in Mark and one of only two long discourses in the Gospel (the other is chapter 13). It is framed by the sea: Jesus sits in a boat to teach at the start and crosses the sea in the same boat at the end, which is why verse 36 says they took him ‘just as he was’. The teaching is built in rings. A narrative frame (1-2, 33-34) encloses two groups of seed parables (3-9 and 26-32), and between them stand the private conversation about the purpose of parables (10-12), the explanation of the sower (13-20), and the paired sayings about the lamp and the measure (21-25). The center of gravity is the call to hear. The verb akouō occurs thirteen times in the chapter: the parable opens with ‘Listen’ (verse 3), the refrain ‘He who has ears to hear, let him hear’ comes twice (9, 23), and the warning to pay attention to what one hears (24) turns the lesson back on the reader.

The three seed parables form a progression. The sower concerns the reception of the word and ends with a harvest; the seed that grows by itself (26-29), the only parable found in Mark alone, concerns the hidden time between sowing and reaping; the mustard seed (30-32) concerns the contrast between a tiny beginning and a great end. All three move from the hidden to the manifest, which is what the lamp saying says outright: nothing is hidden except to be brought to light (22).

The storm scene is told with Mark's typical vivid detail (other boats, the stern, the cushion) and turns on repetition. The Greek describes a great storm (lailaps megalē, 37), a great calm (galēnē megalē, 39), and great fear (phobon megan, 41): the disciples are more afraid after the calm than during the storm. Jesus rebukes the wind and commands the sea to be silent with the same verbs he used on the unclean spirit in the synagogue at Capernaum (1:25), so that the storm is treated as a hostile power. The closing question is left unanswered, and Mark lets the reader carry it into the next scene, where a demon gives an answer the disciples cannot (5:7).

outline.t: A lamp on a stand and the measure you use
The seed that grows by itself

doctrines.note: God's kingdom begins small and hidden, like seed in the ground or a mustard seed, and grows by God's power rather than human effort to a great harvest. The farmer in verses 26 to 29 sleeps and rises and does not know how the seed grows; the earth produces the crop all by itself, and the harvest comes in God's time.

God reveals himself through his word, but hearing is not automatic. The same word falls on different soils, and those who receive it are given more (verses 24 and 25). The mystery of the kingdom is given (verse 11), a divine passive that marks understanding as a gift, and the lamp saying promises that what is hidden now will be brought to light.

Verses 11 and 12 apply Isaiah's commission (Isaiah 6:9-10) to Jesus' parables: God's word both reveals and hardens. The chapter holds this together with real human responsibility, since every soil is described by what it does with the word and the refrain is a command to hear. Christians have weighed the two differently (see the first hard question).

The storm scene shows the two sides of the one person the church confesses. Jesus is tired enough to sleep through a gale in the stern of a fishing boat, and then he rebukes wind and sea as only the Lord does in the Psalms (Psalm 89:9, 107:29). The disciples' question, who is this, is the question the Council of Chalcedon (451) answered: one Lord, truly human and truly God.

Jesus asks his terrified disciples, “Do you still have no faith?” Faith here is trust in Jesus' care and power even when he seems to be asleep, and the storm shows how quickly fear displaces it. Mark does not hide that the insiders who were given the mystery are the ones who fail this test.

words.note: Parabolē, parable. It occurs about 50 times in the New Testament, all but two of them in Matthew, Mark, and Luke (the exceptions are Hebrews 9:9 and 11:19, where it means a figure or type), and eight times in this chapter. The Greek Old Testament uses it to translate mashal, and BDAG notes that its range in the Gospels runs from a full story to a short figurative saying or a riddle (Mark 3:23, 7:17). In Mark it names a mode of speech that both discloses and conceals: open to those who come and ask, opaque to those who stand at a distance.

Mystērion, mystery or secret. It occurs 28 times in the New Testament, but only here and in the parallels (Matthew 13:11, Luke 8:10) in the Gospels; Paul uses it most. It entered biblical Greek in Daniel 2, where it translates the Aramaic raz, the secret of God's purposes that only God can reveal (Daniel 2:28), and the Dead Sea Scrolls use raz the same way. It does not mean a puzzle or a secret rite but a purpose once hidden and now disclosed: that God's reign has arrived in Jesus in a hidden and unexpected form.

Akouō, to hear, listen, heed. It occurs over 400 times in the New Testament and thirteen times in this chapter, more than any other significant word in it. Like the Hebrew shama', the root of the Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4), it can mean simply to perceive sound or to listen with the intent to obey. The whole chapter plays on that range: all four soils hear the word (15, 16, 18, 20), but only the last hear in a way that receives it and bears fruit.

Logos, word. It occurs about 330 times in the New Testament, and in verses 14 to 20 and 33 Mark uses it nine times in its early Christian sense of the message about God's kingdom, the gospel preached (compare 2:2 and Acts 8:4). The explanation of the sower speaks of the word being sown, taken away, received, and choked, so that the parable becomes a description of preaching and its reception, including the preaching Mark's first readers had heard.

Automatos, by itself, of its own accord. It occurs only twice in the New Testament: here, where the earth produces the crop all by itself (verse 28), and in Acts 12:10, where the prison gate opens for Peter of its own accord. The Greek Old Testament uses it for what grows untended in the sabbatical year (Leviticus 25:5). It does not deny the farmer's work, since he sows and reaps, but it places the growth outside his control and knowledge. Paul makes the same point in 1 Corinthians 3:6: “I planted the seed and Apollos watered it, but God made it grow.”

Sinapi, mustard. It occurs five times in the New Testament, always in Jesus' sayings about the mustard seed as the smallest of things (Matthew 13:31, 17:20; Luke 13:19, 17:6). Mark calls the grown plant the largest of garden plants (lachanon), not a tree as Matthew and Luke do, which is closer to botany, and its branches give shade to birds. The image of birds nesting in branches echoes the great trees of Ezekiel 17:23 and Daniel 4:12, pictures of kingdoms that shelter the nations, applied here with a smile to a garden shrub.

Phimoō, to muzzle, to silence. It occurs eight times in the New Testament: literally of muzzling an ox (1 Corinthians 9:9, 1 Timothy 5:18) and figuratively of reducing someone to silence (Matthew 22:12, 34; 1 Peter 2:15). In Mark it is used only in commands of Jesus, to the unclean spirit (1:25) and here to the sea, in the perfect passive imperative pephimōso, ‘be muzzled’ or ‘be still’. The shared verb, together with rebuked (epitimaō) in both places, presents the storm as a power opposed to God that Jesus silences like a demon.

Deilos, cowardly, timid. It occurs only three times in the New Testament: in the parallel Matthew 8:26, here, and in Revelation 21:8, where the cowardly head the list of those who have no share in the new creation. It is a sharper word than afraid; BDAG glosses it as cowardly or fearful. Jesus' question pairs it with faith, and the chapter's last verse turns from this fear of the storm to a different fear, the awe of those who have seen that the wind and sea obey (hupakouō) him, the verb used when the unclean spirits obey him in 1:27.

christ:
In the Old Testament, stilling the sea is something only God does. Psalm 107 describes sailors in a storm who cry to the Lord, and “He calmed the storm to a whisper, and the waves of the sea were hushed” (Psalm 107:29). Psalm 89:9 says to the Lord, “You rule the raging sea; when its waves mount up, You still them,” and in the creation and exodus psalms God rebukes the waters (Psalm 104:7, 106:9). When Jesus rebukes the wind and it obeys, the disciples are right to be more afraid after the calm than during the storm: they are in the boat with someone who does what God does. Mark does not answer their question in so many words, but the answer is written into the scene for anyone who knows the Psalms.

The scene also echoes Jonah, asleep in the ship while the Lord hurled a great wind on the sea (Jonah 1:4-6). The Greek of Mark 4:41, they feared a great fear, repeats the words of the Greek Jonah 1:10 and 1:16 about the sailors. The contrast is as important as the likeness. Jonah slept because he was fleeing God and was thrown overboard to calm the sea; Jesus sleeps in trust (compare Psalm 4:8) and calms the sea by his word. Jesus himself later calls his death and resurrection the sign of Jonah (Matthew 12:39-41), and some interpreters hear in the sleeping and rising a first glimpse of that. Psalm 44:23 cries “Wake up, O Lord! Why are You sleeping?”, and the disciples' cry in verse 38 is that psalm's complaint on the lips of frightened men.

In the parables Jesus is the sower of the word, and the kingdom whose hidden beginnings he describes is present in his own ministry, small and resisted in Galilee and destined for a harvest. The last parable borrows the prophets' images of harvest (Joel 3:13, “Swing the sickle, for the harvest is ripe”) and of a great tree where birds nest (Ezekiel 17:23, Daniel 4:12), so that Jesus places his small beginnings inside Israel's hope for the day when God's reign would shelter the nations. The quotation of Isaiah 6 does the same with judgment: Isaiah's word hardened a people until only a stump was left, and Isaiah 6:13 calls that stump the holy seed. Jesus' parables of seed come out of that same prophetic story.
interpretation:
Early Christian readers found in the chapter a picture of the church. Tertullian (On Baptism 12, around 200) says the little boat was a figure of the church, tossed in the sea of the world by the waves of persecution and temptation while the Lord seems to sleep, until roused by the prayers of the saints he calms the world for his own. Augustine (Sermon 63, preached on Matthew's version) turned the scene inward: Christ asleep in the boat is faith asleep in the heart, and a Christian insulted and rising in anger should wake Christ by remembering his word. The sower was read as a map of hearers from the fathers onward, and the three yields were often allegorized; Jerome (Against Jovinian 1.3, around 393) matched the hundredfold, sixtyfold, and thirtyfold to virgins, widows, and the married, a reading later interpreters rejected as foreign to the parable. Augustine's judgment that Mark was a follower and abbreviator of Matthew (Harmony of the Gospels 1.2.4) meant that Mark was rarely commented on for its own sake; Bede's commentary on Mark (written after 716) and Theophylact of Ohrid's (late eleventh century) are the main medieval exceptions, and Bede reads the other boats of verse 36 as believers not yet tested by tribulation.

The Reformers pressed the parables toward the power of the preached word. Luther, returning to Wittenberg in March 1522 to calm the unrest of the radical reformers, told his congregation in the Invocavit sermons that he had only preached and written God's word, and that while he slept or drank Wittenberg beer with Philip Melanchthon and Nicholas von Amsdorf, the word did the work, an unmistakable echo of the seed that grows while the farmer sleeps. Calvin, in his Harmony of the Gospels, read verses 11 and 12 as God's just judgment on the reprobate and the gift of understanding as grace to the elect.

Modern study of the parables began with Adolf Jülicher (Die Gleichnisreden Jesu, 1888 and 1899), who argued that each parable makes one point and that allegorical explanations such as verses 13 to 20 came from the church. C. H. Dodd (The Parables of the Kingdom, 1935) read the parables as announcing a kingdom already present, and Joachim Jeremias (Die Gleichnisse Jesu, 1947) placed them in Jesus' own conflicts. Later scholars, among them Birger Gerhardsson, Craig Blomberg (Interpreting the Parables, 1990), and Klyne Snodgrass (Stories with Intent, 2008), argued that Jewish parables often carried interpretations, so an explanation like this one fits Jesus' setting. Joel Marcus (The Mystery of the Kingdom of God, 1986) read the chapter against Jewish apocalyptic, and the literary critic Frank Kermode (The Genesis of Secrecy, 1979) made verses 11 and 12 the starting point for a study of how all narratives keep insiders and outsiders. Among Jewish scholars, Flusser and Amy-Jill Levine (Short Stories by Jesus, 2014) have read the parables as the work of a Jewish teacher and warned against readings that make them attacks on Judaism.

In liturgy the Revised Common Lectionary reads verses 26 to 34 and 35 to 41 on consecutive Sundays in June in Year B (Propers 6 and 7), and the Roman Lectionary reads the same passages on the eleventh and twelfth Sundays in Ordinary Time. Rembrandt's The Storm on the Sea of Galilee (1633), his only seascape, shows the boat heeling in the gale with the disciples struggling and Jesus being roused; it was stolen from the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum in Boston in March 1990 and has never been recovered. William Whiting's hymn Eternal Father, Strong to Save (1860), sung in the British and American navies, addresses Christ as the one whose voice the waters heard and who slept calmly amid the storm's rage.
text:
Most differences between English Bibles in this chapter come from manuscripts that the King James Version followed and modern versions do not. In verse 40 the earliest witnesses, including Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, read oupō, ‘not yet’ or ‘still’: “Do you still have no faith?” Most later manuscripts read pōs ouk, which the King James Version renders ‘how is it that ye have no faith?’. The earlier reading is the sharper one and implies that faith should have grown by now. In verse 12 later manuscripts add ‘their sins’ (‘and their sins should be forgiven them’, KJV), filling out a short phrase. In verse 10 the earliest manuscripts have the disciples ask about ‘the parables’ in the plural, a question about Jesus' use of parables in general, while later ones, followed by the KJV, have ‘the parable’. In verses 8 and 20 the Greek letters that introduce each number can be read as ‘one’ (one seed bore thirty) or ‘in’ (it bore in thirties), because early manuscripts had no accents; the sense is unaffected.

There are also translation choices a reader will notice. Verse 38's proskephalaion is ‘the cushion’ in most versions and ‘a pillow’ in the KJV. Verse 39's two commands are ‘Peace, be still’ in the KJV, familiar from hymns, and ‘Silence. Be still’ or ‘Quiet. Be still’ in modern versions; the Greek is literally ‘be silent, be muzzled’. In verse 21 the Greek says literally ‘does the lamp come’ (erchetai), where most versions paraphrase ‘is a lamp brought in’, and some interpreters think the odd verb hints that the lamp is Jesus, who has come.

teach.big: The kingdom of God comes through a word that looks weak and meets resistance, yet grows by God's power to a harvest; those who hear it truly will trust the one who speaks it even when he seems to sleep in the storm.

outline.t: The same word falls on every kind of ground; the losses are real, but the harvest is far larger than the losses.
Understanding is a gift given to those who come near and ask, and refusing to come near is its own judgment.
Four hearings of one word: Satan, trouble, and competing desires are named plainly as the enemies of fruitfulness.
The hidden word is meant to be seen, and how we listen decides how much more we receive.
Growth belongs to God; the sower's task is to sow, wait, and reap, not to make it happen.
Do not despise small beginnings: the smallest seed becomes shelter for others.
Jesus does what only God does, and the fitting response to him moves from panic to awe.

teach.pitfalls:
The most common misreading turns the sower into a lesson on effort: work harder to become good soil. The parable's first point is the sower's extravagant sowing and the certainty of harvest, and it is a comfort to those who preach and see little result as much as a challenge to hearers. A second misreading turns the soils into fixed types of people, so that a listener is labeled once for all as hard or shallow. Mark's own story shows the disciples behaving like several soils in turn, and the call to hear assumes that a hearer can change. Teachers should also avoid resolving verses 11 and 12 too quickly in either direction, either by denying that they speak of judgment or by reading them as a closed decree that makes the call to hear meaningless.

The mustard seed is often preached as a lesson on church growth or numbers. It speaks of God's kingdom, not any one church's success, and its contrast is between hidden beginnings and a sure end. With the storm, the familiar sermon about the storms of life is legitimate as far as it goes, since the church has read the story that way since Tertullian, but it fails the text if it leaves out the chapter's actual question. The point is not first that Jesus will calm your storm but who Jesus is. Avoid, too, promising that faith always brings calm: the disciples were rescued in spite of their lack of faith, not because of its strength, and Mark's first readers in a time of persecution were not all rescued from death.
teach.pastoral: The storm scene will reach people who have prayed and felt that God was asleep. The disciples' words in verse 38 are close to a psalm of lament (Psalm 44:23), and Scripture gives believers permission to speak that way; teach it as honest prayer, not as a failure to be ashamed of. Take care not to tell grieving or anxious people that their fear shows they lack faith, when Jesus' rebuke was spoken to men who had just watched him heal and teach and when he calmed the sea before he said it. The parables of seed may help pastors, parents, and teachers who have labored without visible fruit: the growth is God's, and the farmer is allowed to sleep. The explanation of the sower may also press on people who fell away under trouble or were choked by worry; the chapter does not close the door on them, since its last word to the failing disciples is still a question that invites faith.

hard.q: Does Jesus teach in parables so that people will not understand and be forgiven?
hard.a:
The objection is strong and old. Verse 12 introduces Isaiah 6:9-10 with hina, ‘so that’, and ends with mēpote, ‘lest’ or ‘otherwise’, which on its plainest reading says that Jesus speaks in riddles in order to keep outsiders from repenting and being forgiven. Matthew seems to have felt the difficulty, since he changes ‘so that’ to ‘because’ (Matthew 13:13). Critics have found here a teacher who excludes, or a church that later explained its failure with Israel by claiming it was intended. The literary critic Frank Kermode (The Genesis of Secrecy, 1979) took the verse at its word and built on it an argument that narratives exclude outsiders as surely as they admit insiders, and Joel Marcus (The Mystery of the Kingdom of God, 1986) read Mark's parable theory as a real statement of divine hardening, set within Jewish apocalyptic thought about mysteries revealed to some and hidden from others. In the Reformed tradition Calvin read the verses as God's judgment on the reprobate.

Other readers answer along several lines. Joachim Jeremias (The Parables of Jesus) argued that hina here is shorthand for ‘so that Scripture might be fulfilled’ and that mēpote reflects an Aramaic expression that can mean ‘unless’: unless they repent and are forgiven. He noted that Mark's wording, ‘be forgiven’, agrees with the Aramaic Targum of Isaiah 6:10 against the Hebrew and Greek ‘be healed’, which suggests a Palestinian origin for the saying; Bruce Chilton has also studied the link with the Targum. Many commentators add that in Isaiah the words describe the effect of the prophet's preaching on a people who had already hardened themselves, and that Mark's outsiders are defined by their response, since in 3:31-35 the family stands outside while those around Jesus are inside, and anyone can come and ask, as the disciples do in verse 10. The chapter itself says the parables were spoken to the extent that they could understand (verse 33) and that a lamp is meant for a stand (verse 21). Christians who stress God's sovereign choice and those who stress human freedom have read these verses differently for centuries, and both traditions keep the chapter's constant call to hear.

hard.q: Did Jesus give the explanation of the sower, or did the early church add it?
hard.a:
The case that the explanation is later is set out most fully by Adolf Jülicher (1888 and 1899) and Joachim Jeremias (1947). Jülicher argued that genuine parables make a single comparison and that point-by-point allegory is a sign of later church interpretation. Jeremias added that the vocabulary of verses 14 to 20 (the word used absolutely for the gospel, sowing the word, persecution because of the word, the deceitfulness of riches) is the language of the apostolic mission rather than Jesus' own, and that the explanation shifts the parable's emphasis from the harvest to the hearers' psychology. Many critical scholars have followed them, and the Gospel of Thomas (saying 9) has the parable without any explanation.

Others reply that Jülicher's single-point rule does not fit the evidence of ancient parables. Jewish parables, including the rabbinic meshalim studied by David Flusser (1981), often carry explanations and allegorical details, and the Old Testament's parables of the vineyard (Isaiah 5:1-7) and the eagles (Ezekiel 17) come with interpretations attached. Birger Gerhardsson, Craig Blomberg (Interpreting the Parables, 1990), and Klyne Snodgrass (Stories with Intent, 2008) have argued that an explanation of this kind fits a Jewish teacher training disciples, that sowing is already an Old Testament image for God's word and people (Isaiah 55:10-11, Jeremiah 31:27), and that vocabulary shared with early Christian preaching may show where the church learned its language rather than where it invented Jesus'. The question is historical, not doctrinal, and believers who hold a high view of Scripture have usually read the explanation as Jesus' own, as Mark presents it. Either way the explanation shows how Mark wanted his readers to hear the parable: as a searching word about their own hearing.

observe: What happens to the seed on each of the four kinds of ground, and what does Jesus say each represents in verses 14 to 20?
What does the farmer in verses 26 to 29 do, and what does he not know or do?
What do the disciples say to Jesus when they wake him, and what two questions does he ask them afterward?
interpret: Why do you think Jesus quotes Isaiah 6 to explain his parables, and how does the rest of the chapter (verses 21 to 25 and 33) shape the meaning of that quotation?
What do the three seed parables together say about how God's kingdom arrives and grows?
Why are the disciples more afraid after the calm than during the storm, and what does their question in verse 41 show they are beginning to see?
apply: Which of the dangers in verses 15 to 19 (the word snatched away, trouble, worries, wealth, other desires) presses hardest on your hearing of God's word now?
Where are you tempted to measure God's work by visible results, and how does the seed that grows by itself free you to sow and wait?
When has God seemed asleep to you? How might the disciples' honest cry, and Jesus' answer, shape the way you pray in that place?
